name: Anıtkabir
desc: Atatürk's mausoleum crowns a hill above the city, approached along a 262-metre avenue lined with Hittite-style stone lions. The scale is deliberately calm rather than grandiose: pale travertine colonnades, a huge empty ceremonial court, and a guard change performed with unnerving slowness. The museum beneath the terrace covers the War of Independence in real detail.
season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Oct — the ceremonial court has zero shade in August
tip: Time your walk up the Lion Road for the guard change on the hour, then go underground to the museum almost every day-tripper skips.
todo: Walk the Lion Road end to end
Watch the changing of the guard
See the War of Independence panorama
rev: Visitors consistently find it more affecting than expected, but complain about the airport-style bag check at the gate and staff turning away anyone in shorts or a hat on the court.
onward: Ankara Esenboğa (ESB) airport, then the Belko Air bus to Kızılay and the M2 metro to Tandoğan, ten minutes uphill on foot.

name: Museum of Anatolian Civilizations
desc: Two restored Ottoman buildings below the castle hold the best Hittite collection anywhere: the Çatalhöyük wall paintings, the Alacahöyük bronze standards, and orthostat reliefs of gods in pointed hats carried off the walls of Karkamış. It is compact enough to do properly in two hours and rearranged chronologically, so Anatolia's ten thousand years finally line up.
season: Year-round — an obvious refuge on a wet or freezing Ankara day
tip: Do this before Çatalhöyük or Gordion, not after; the finds are all here and the sites themselves are bare earth without them.
todo: Find the Çatalhöyük leopard shrine wall
Study the Hittite orthostat reliefs
Walk up to the castle gate after
rev: Widely rated Türkiye's finest museum, though the foreigner ticket price has climbed steeply and school groups can make the Hittite hall genuinely loud by mid-morning.
onward: Ankara Esenboğa (ESB) airport, then metro to Ulus and a fifteen-minute walk uphill through the Atpazarı copper market.

name: Ankara Castle
desc: Byzantine walls built from recycled Roman marble — column drums and inscribed blocks jammed straight into the masonry — enclose a living quarter of leaning timber houses, laundry lines and cats. Climb to the Şark Kulesi and the whole grey sprawl of Ankara opens out, with the citadel's own tiled roofs directly below.
season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Nov — the cobbles ice over in winter
tip: Go up an hour before sunset and buy dried fruit and pastırma in the Atpazarı lanes on the way back down, when the spice sellers are still open.
todo: Climb the Şark Kulesi for the view
Spot Roman spolia in the walls
Eat at a rooftop in the citadel
rev: People love the ramshackle village-inside-a-city feel but warn that the summit has no railings in places, the lanes are steep and slippery, and several 'historic' konak restaurants are tourist-priced.
onward: Ankara Esenboğa (ESB) airport, then metro to Ulus; walk uphill through Atpazarı or take a taxi to the Parmak Kapı gate.

name: Hamamönü
desc: A block of Ottoman Ankara restored back from near-collapse: bay-windowed timber houses in ochre and dusty green, a restored hamam, and courtyards selling handicrafts and mantı. It is frankly a curated version of the past, but the street width, the overhanging upper floors and the smell of woodsmoke in autumn are the real thing.
season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Oct — Ramadan evenings are the liveliest, and coldest in Jan
tip: Skip the main Hacı Musa street cafés and cut into the side lanes behind the Karacabey hamam, where the restoration stops and the original neighbourhood carries on.
todo: Drink şıra in a konak courtyard
See Mehmet Akif Ersoy's house
Browse the craft workshops
rev: Ankara residents rate it a pleasant evening stroll; travellers who arrive expecting Safranbolu find it small, heavily made-over, and dead on a weekday morning.
onward: Ankara Esenboğa (ESB) airport, then metro to Ulus or Kızılay and a fifteen-minute walk or short taxi to Hacettepe.

name: Hacı Bayram Mosque
desc: Ankara's most-visited religious building, a fifteenth-century mosque of brick and Kütahya tile built hard against a Roman temple wall. The square outside is the city's warmest public space: families feeding pigeons, women selling rosaries and boiled corn, and a steady traffic of pilgrims to the tomb of the poet-saint Hacı Bayram Veli.
season: Year-round — Friday midday and religious holidays are packed
tip: Walk around the back of the mosque to where the Ottoman brickwork meets the Roman ashlar; the seam between the two is a metre from your hand.
todo: Visit the tomb of Hacı Bayram Veli
Buy roasted chickpeas on the square
See the Roman wall behind
rev: Visitors find the atmosphere genuinely devotional rather than touristic, though the square is crowded, the surrounding streets are shabby, and modest dress plus headscarves for women are enforced.
onward: Ankara Esenboğa (ESB) airport, then metro to Ulus and five minutes on foot uphill.

name: Temple of Augustus and Rome
desc: The single most important Latin inscription in the world sits in a scruffy yard behind a mosque in Ankara. The Res Gestae Divi Augusti — the emperor's own account of his reign — is carved on the inner cella walls in Latin, with a Greek translation on the outside. Roofless, weathered, and almost entirely ignored by the crowds twenty metres away.
season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Oct — legible light is better on an overcast day
tip: The Greek text on the exterior south wall is far easier to read than the Latin inside; bring a photo of the translation because there is next to no interpretation on site.
todo: Read the Res Gestae on the cella wall
Find the Greek version outside
Combine with Hacı Bayram next door
rev: Classicists call it unmissable; everyone else reports a fenced, weedy enclosure with almost no signage and periodic closure for restoration scaffolding.
onward: Ankara Esenboğa (ESB) airport, then metro to Ulus; the temple shares a courtyard with Hacı Bayram Mosque.

name: Gordion
desc: The Phrygian capital where Alexander cut the knot, now a low citadel mound in wheat country with nearly a hundred burial tumuli scattered around it. The Midas Mound is the reason to come: a tunnel drilled through 50 metres of earth ends at the oldest standing wooden building on earth, a juniper and pine chamber sealed around 740 BC.
season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Oct — the plain is a furnace in July and August
tip: The tumulus tunnel is cool, damp and unlit in places, and the little site museum holds the inlaid furniture found inside — do museum, tumulus, then citadel, in that order.
todo: Walk into the Midas Mound tunnel
See the inlaid Phrygian furniture
Climb the citadel gate ramp
rev: Newly inscribed by UNESCO and still refreshingly empty, though visitors note the citadel itself is bare stone footings, signage is thin, and there is no shade or café anywhere near.
entry: ₺300 (≈€6) for museum, tumulus and site · covered by Museum Pass Türkiye
onward: Ankara Esenboğa (ESB) airport, then 95 km west via Polatlı; there are buses to Polatlı but the last 18 km to Yassıhöyük really needs a car or taxi.

name: Beypazarı
desc: A weekend town of white Ottoman houses stacked up a hillside, restored before the fashion for it and still half working town. The local trade is silver filigree, carrots, and a many-layered baklava made with 80 sheets of pastry. Above it, the İnözü valley cuts through soft rock full of Byzantine cave chambers.
season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Oct — weekdays if you want the streets to yourself
tip: Skip the main square restaurants and eat tarhana soup and kuru dolma at a house-restaurant in the back lanes, then drive fifteen minutes into İnözü valley for the caves.
todo: Eat 80-layer Beypazarı baklava
Watch a silver filigree workshop
Drive into the İnözü valley
rev: Charming and genuinely well restored, but on Saturdays and Sundays it fills with Ankara coach parties and the historic streets become a queue for photos and carrot juice.
entry: Free (town) · small fee for the Living Museum house
onward: Ankara Esenboğa (ESB) airport, then 100 km northwest on the D140; frequent minibuses run from Ankara AŞTİ, taking about ninety minutes.

name: Nallıhan Bird Sanctuary
desc: Where the Sarıyar reservoir backs up against bare striped hills, a shallow marsh has become one of inland Anatolia's best bird stops — around 170 species logged, including flamingos, black storks and pygmy cormorants. There is a wooden hide and an observation terrace above the water, and generally nobody else in it.
season: Mar–May and Sep–Nov for migration; the marsh shrinks badly by August
tip: Bring your own binoculars and go at first light — by ten the heat haze off the reservoir wrecks the viewing and the birds are gone from the shallows.
todo: Sit out an hour in the hide
Scan the shallows for flamingos
Climb to the terrace viewpoint
rev: Birders rate it highly in spring passage, but casual visitors often arrive at midday, see distant specks, and find the access track dusty and the facilities minimal.
onward: Ankara Esenboğa (ESB) airport, then 160 km west via Beypazarı to Davutoğlan; a car is essentially required.

name: Nallıhan Coloured Hills
desc: Bands of red, ochre, violet and pale green run across bare eroded ridges above the Sarıyar reservoir — lignite, clay and iron oxide laid down in an old lake bed and stripped naked by the wind. From the Davutoğlan viewpoint the striping runs for kilometres with the blue reservoir underneath it.
season: Mar–May and Oct–Nov — colour saturates after rain and in low sun
tip: Late afternoon light lifts the reds; at midday the whole ridge goes flat and grey, which is why most people's photos are disappointing.
todo: Drive the ridge road above the reservoir
Shoot the stripes in late light
Pair with the bird sanctuary below
rev: Photographers travel from Ankara for it and rarely regret the trip, though the tracks up to the best angles are unpaved, unsigned and rutted enough to worry a low hire car.
onward: Ankara Esenboğa (ESB) airport, then 160 km west via Beypazarı; no public transport reaches the viewpoints.

name: Soğuksu National Park & Kızılcahamam
desc: Black pine and fir forest an hour north of Ankara, cool when the city is at 38 °C, with black vultures nesting on the cliffs and marked trails to the Çamlıdere viewpoints. The spa town of Kızılcahamam sits at its edge, all thermal hotels and mineral water so carbonated that locals bottle it straight from the roadside fountains.
season: May–Oct for the forest; Dec–Feb for snow and a hot pool
tip: Fill a bottle at the maden suyu spring in Kızılcahamam — it is naturally fizzy, faintly metallic, and free — then drive up to Soğuksu before the Sunday picnic crowd arrives.
todo: Walk to the Çamkoru forest trail
Soak in a thermal pool
Drink the fizzy spring water
rev: Ankara's default escape, praised for clean air and cheap thermal hotels; complaints centre on weekend picnic litter, mediocre hotel food, and the park being a park rather than wilderness.
entry: Small vehicle fee for the national park · thermal pools charged separately
onward: Ankara Esenboğa (ESB) airport, then 60 km north on the O-4 / D750; regular buses run from Ankara AŞTİ to Kızılcahamam.

name: Ayaş
desc: A quiet market town of timber-framed houses forty minutes west of Ankara, known for its tomatoes, its vine leaves, and a hot spring in the valley below at Ayaş İçmece. The old quarter around the Ulu Cami has the same bones as Beypazarı with none of the coach parties, and half the konaks are still lived in.
season: May–Oct — the tomato season peaks Aug–Sep and the market is at its best
tip: Come on a Friday for the market and buy Ayaş tomatoes by the crate; they are the reason Ankara households drive out here at all.
todo: Walk the old konak streets
Buy tomatoes at the Friday market
Take the waters at Ayaş İçmece
rev: Those who make the detour like the total absence of tourism, but there is little restored, few places to eat well, and the thermal facilities are basic municipal ones.
onward: Ankara Esenboğa (ESB) airport, then 60 km west on the D140 towards Beypazarı; minibuses run from Ankara AŞTİ.

name: Lake Eymir
desc: A long reedy lake in a fold of steppe on Ankara's southern edge, held by METU university and therefore protected from development. A flat 7-kilometre track runs the shore under poplars, rowing eights train on the water in the evening, and cormorants sit out on the dead trees. It is the closest thing Ankara has to a green lung.
season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Oct — the poplars turn gold in late October
tip: Enter from the Gölbaşı side and go on a weekday; weekend afternoons the loop fills with cyclists and the car park closes when full.
todo: Cycle the full shore loop
Watch the rowers at dusk
Have tea at the boathouse
rev: Ankara's favourite easy walk, though visitors mention restricted entry hours, occasional algal smell in late summer, and the fact that swimming is not allowed.
entry: Free on foot · small charge for cars
onward: Ankara Esenboğa (ESB) airport, then 25 km south past Gölbaşı; city buses run to Gölbaşı and the entrance is a short taxi from there.

name: Odunpazarı
desc: Eskişehir's Ottoman quarter: narrow cobbled lanes of timber houses painted lilac, mustard and turquoise, climbing a low hill above the modern city. Meerschaum — the soft white stone carved into pipes here for two centuries — is sold in every second shop. The stacked-timber OMM modern art museum at the bottom of the hill is a genuinely good building.
season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Oct — Eskişehir winters are grey and bitter
tip: Buy meerschaum from a workshop where someone is actually carving; the polished 'antique' pipes in the souvenir shops are mostly pressed dust, not block stone.
todo: Watch a meerschaum carver at work
Visit the OMM museum
Eat çiğ börek in the lanes
rev: Students and weekenders love the colour and the cafés; the recurring gripe is that the restoration has tipped into theme-park, with too many identical gift shops and inflated café prices.
onward: Ankara Esenboğa (ESB) or Istanbul, then the YHT high-speed train to Eskişehir — the station is a 20-minute walk from Odunpazarı.

name: The Porsuk in Eskişehir
desc: A modest brown river that a determined mayor turned into the spine of the city: willow-lined embankments, a string of low bridges, gondolas poled by students, and cafés with their chairs at the water's edge. On a summer evening the whole of Eskişehir is walking along it, and the Adalar strip is one of the most sociable places in inland Türkiye.
season: May–Sep evenings — the gondolas stop running in the cold months
tip: Take the gondola upstream at dusk rather than the daytime run, and eat çiğ börek at a stand-up place off Hamamyolu instead of a riverside terrace.
todo: Ride a Porsuk gondola at dusk
Walk Hamamyolu to the Adalar
Try Eskişehir çiğ börek
rev: Turks routinely call Eskişehir the country's most liveable city because of this river, while visitors point out the water itself is murky, the gondola ride is short, and the copycat cafés blur together.
onward: Ankara or Istanbul, then the YHT high-speed train to Eskişehir; the riverfront starts five minutes from the station.

name: Midas City & the Phrygian Valley
desc: A 17-metre rock façade carved with a geometric lattice and the name MIDAI stands above a village of poplar trees, and behind it a plateau of tunnelled stairways, rock altars and cult niches. The wider Phrygian Valley runs south through Han and Ihsaniye in tufa canyons and fairy chimneys — Cappadocia's landscape with a thousandth of the traffic.
season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Oct — snow closes the plateau tracks in winter
tip: Take the dark stepped tunnel down through the rock behind the monument — it is unlit, you need a phone torch, and almost nobody finds it.
todo: Stand under the Midas Monument façade
Descend the rock-cut stair tunnel
Drive the valley to Ayazini
rev: Those who make it call the emptiness the whole point, but expect an unstaffed site, patchy signage, a long unpaved approach, and nowhere to buy so much as water.
onward: Eskişehir by YHT train, then 80 km south via Seyitgazi and Han on the D260; there is no useful bus and you need a car.

name: Seyitgazi Complex
desc: A Seljuk and Ottoman complex piled on a rock spur above a small town, built around the tomb of an eighth-century Arab warrior-saint and, beside it, an improbably long sarcophagus said to hold a Byzantine princess who loved him. Dervish cells, a mosque and a cavernous kitchen ring the courtyard, and pilgrims still tie cloth to the window grilles.
season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Oct — exposed and freezing on the spur in winter
tip: Combine it with Midas City in one loop south from Eskişehir; the two are 30 km apart and both need a car anyway.
todo: See the two tombs side by side
Walk the dervish cell courtyard
Look down over the town from the wall
rev: Visitors describe an atmospheric, still-functioning shrine rather than a museum, with the caveats that opening hours are erratic, restoration works recur, and English information is essentially absent.
entry: Free · donations expected at the tomb
onward: Eskişehir by YHT train, then 45 km south on the D260; minibuses run from Eskişehir but leave you a walk up to the complex.

name: Sivrihisar
desc: A town wedged under jagged quartzite crags with one extraordinary building: the thirteenth-century Ulu Cami, whose flat roof rests on 67 wooden columns with reused Byzantine capitals — one of the wooden hypostyle mosques now on the UNESCO list. Around it are an Armenian church, an Ottoman clock tower, and a statue of Nasreddin Hoca on his donkey, backwards.
season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Oct — the crags glow at sunset
tip: Ask at the mosque for the light switch; the forest of painted columns is almost invisible until someone turns the interior lights on.
todo: Stand among the 67 wooden columns
Climb towards the crags for the view
Detour to Pessinus at Ballıhisar
rev: The mosque interior astonishes people who stopped only for lunch on the Ankara road; the town itself is sleepy, with limited food options and a scruffy main street.
onward: Eskişehir or Ankara, then the D200 highway — Sivrihisar sits directly on it, roughly halfway between the two, and all intercity buses stop here.

name: Pessinus
desc: The cult centre of Cybele, from where the black meteorite of the Great Mother was shipped to Rome in 204 BC. What survives in the fields of Ballıhisar village is a stepped theatre-like structure, a canalised stream lined with cut blocks, and a temple platform — plus columns and sarcophagi propped against village walls. Ancient stone lying about in a working farm hamlet.
season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Oct — mud in spring, stubble and heat in summer
tip: Walk the length of the stone-lined canal through the village; it is the most complete thing on site and nothing directs you to it.
todo: Walk the marble-lined canal
Find the stepped temple platform
Spot spolia in the village walls
rev: Ancient-history readers find it moving to stand where Cybele's cult began; everyone else reports scattered rubble, no fence, no guide, and a rough 15 km track off the highway.
onward: Eskişehir or Ankara to Sivrihisar on the D200, then 13 km south on a minor road to Ballıhisar; a car is required.

name: Sakarbaşı Springs
desc: The Sakarya, one of Türkiye's great rivers, starts here as a set of turquoise spring pools bubbling up through white sand in a flat field near Çifteler. The water is startlingly clear and cold, watercress grows in the outflow, and within a few hundred metres it is already a proper river running north.
season: May–Sep — the colour is best in strong overhead light
tip: The pools are on the Çifteler stud farm road and easy to drive past; look for the picnic grove and follow the concrete channel upstream to the boils.
todo: Watch the sand boil in the spring pools
Follow the channel to the river
Picnic under the poplars
rev: A pleasant, genuinely pretty half-hour that Turkish families rate for picnics, though visitors note litter around the picnic tables and that swimming in the springs is prohibited.
onward: Eskişehir by YHT train, then 60 km southeast via Mahmudiye to Çifteler; minibuses run to Çifteler town but the springs need a taxi or car.

name: Balıkdamı Wetland
desc: Where the Sakarya slows and spreads into reed beds south of Sivrihisar, over 200 bird species have been recorded — cranes, glossy ibis, purple heron, and a heavy spring passage of waders. It is flat, wet, mosquito-ridden and completely undeveloped, which is exactly why the birds are there.
season: Mar–May and Sep–Nov — dry and dull by late summer
tip: Go at dawn, wear boots, and bring insect repellent; the tracks between the reed beds flood after rain and there is no hide worth the name.
todo: Scan the reed beds for cranes
Walk the dyke path at first light
Count waders on spring passage
rev: Serious birders rate it among inland Türkiye's best wetlands; casual visitors find muddy tracks, no facilities, aggressive mosquitoes and shooting pressure in autumn.
onward: Eskişehir or Ankara to Sivrihisar on the D200, then about 25 km south on village roads; a car with some clearance is sensible.

name: Mevlâna Museum
desc: Rumi's tomb under a fluted turquoise-tiled cone, the most recognisable roofline in Konya. Inside, a low-lit hall of sarcophagi wrapped in embroidered cloth, dervish felt hats, illuminated Masnavi manuscripts and a case holding a hair of the Prophet. Visitors move slowly and many are praying; it functions as a shrine that happens to sell tickets.
season: Year-round — 17 December, the Şeb-i Arus, is the annual peak and books out
tip: Arrive at opening, before the coach groups; and if you want to see the sema properly, book the Mevlana Cultural Centre performance rather than the restaurant versions.
todo: See the Masnavi manuscripts
Walk the dervish cell rooms
Watch a sema at the culture centre
rev: Almost universally described as atmospheric and worth the trip, with the usual complaints about shoe-cover queues, dense crowds by 11am, and a strict no-photo rule in the tomb chamber.
onward: Konya (KYA) airport or the YHT high-speed train from Ankara or Istanbul, then the tram along Mevlana Caddesi to the Mevlana stop.

name: Alâeddin Hill
desc: An artificial mound in the middle of Konya, occupied since the Bronze Age, now a park of old plane trees with the Seljuk sultans' mosque on top. The Alâeddin Mosque is a strange, austere hall of mismatched antique columns; beside it stand the ruined arch of the Seljuk palace and a tomb chamber holding eight sultans.
season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Oct — the plane trees give real shade in summer
tip: Cross the road afterwards to the Karatay Medrese, whose tiled dome of star-and-cross mosaic is the single most beautiful ceiling in the city and takes twenty minutes.
todo: Sit under the columns in the mosque
Find the sultans' tomb chamber
Cross to the Karatay Medrese
rev: Locals treat it as the city's living room and visitors like that; the mosque interior is often shut outside prayer times and the surviving palace arch is a disappointing sliver under a canopy.
entry: Free (mosque and park) · Karatay Medrese small fee
onward: Konya (KYA) airport or YHT train, then the tram to Alaaddin — the hill is the tram's own loop.

name: Çatalhöyük
desc: A 9,000-year-old town where people entered their mud-brick houses through the roof, buried their dead under the floors and painted bulls on the walls — one of the first places humans lived densely without streets. Two shelters cover the excavation trenches, and a reconstructed house lets you climb down a ladder into a Neolithic room.
season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Oct — the Konya plain hits 38 °C with no shade in summer
tip: The finds are in Konya and Ankara, not here — read the site panels first, then look at the trench, or it will read as a pit of mud walls.
todo: Climb into the reconstructed house
Look down into the north shelter trench
Walk the mound perimeter path
rev: Archaeology-minded visitors find it genuinely stirring, but many others report a long flat drive, a small visitor centre, and mud-brick trenches that need imagination to read.
onward: Konya (KYA) airport or YHT train, then 50 km southeast via Çumra; buses reach Çumra but the last 10 km needs a taxi.

name: Sille
desc: A Greek-Orthodox village swallowed by Konya's suburbs but still intact in its gorge: stone houses on both banks of a dry stream, rock-cut chapels in the cliff, and the Aya Elenia church with its painted iconostasis, said to have been founded by Constantine's mother. The Greeks left in 1924; the village kept its bones.
season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Nov — pretty under snow but slippery
tip: Walk uphill past the last café to the rock-cut chapels above the village, where the frescoes are faint but the graffiti goes back centuries and nobody follows you.
todo: See the iconostasis in Aya Elenia
Climb to the cave chapels
Have gözleme by the stream
rev: A rewarding half-day from Konya, though the stream bed is dry and concreted, the café strip is aimed squarely at weekenders, and the church keeps unreliable hours.
entry: Small fee for the church — under €2
onward: Konya (KYA) airport or YHT train, then city bus 64 from Konya centre, about 8 km northwest, roughly 25 minutes.

name: Lake Beyşehir
desc: Türkiye's largest freshwater lake, shallow and pale blue with the Anamas and Dedegöl mountains standing behind it and around thirty islands, some with ruined Byzantine churches. Fishermen sell pike-perch on the quay at Beyşehir town, and the west shore road towards Kubad Abad runs through apple orchards with the water on one side the whole way.
season: May–Sep for the lake; Oct for clear air and empty shores
tip: Hire a boat from Beyşehir quay in the morning to reach Kız Adası and Mada island — afternoon wind gets up and the boatmen stop going out.
todo: Take a boat to the lake islands
Eat sudak fish on the quay
Drive the west shore to Kubad Abad
rev: Loved for its scale and its fish restaurants, but water levels have dropped badly in dry years, some shoreline is reedy and hard to reach, and the town itself is unremarkable.
entry: Free · boat trips roughly ₺500–1000 (≈€10–20) per boat
onward: Konya (KYA) airport, then 90 km west on the D330; regular buses run Konya–Beyşehir in about ninety minutes.

name: Eşrefoğlu Mosque
desc: Forty-eight cedar columns hold up a flat wooden ceiling in near-darkness, lit by a single opening above a sunken snow well in the floor. Built in 1299, it is the largest and best preserved of the wooden hypostyle mosques of medieval Anatolia, with an original carved minbar and a mihrab of turquoise and black tile.
season: Year-round — snow falling through the roof opening in winter is the point
tip: Go in winter if you can: the light shaft over the karlık is designed so snow drops in and melts to humidify the wood, and it is the reason the beams have survived seven centuries.
todo: Look up at the painted wooden ceiling
Find the snow well under the light shaft
Study the carved walnut minbar
rev: People repeatedly say it beats far more famous mosques, with the caveats that it is very dark for photography, closed to visitors during prayers, and modest dress is enforced.
entry: Free · donation box at the door
onward: Konya (KYA) airport, then 90 km west to Beyşehir town centre; the mosque is a five-minute walk from the bus station.

name: Kubad Abad Palace
desc: The lakeside summer palace of Sultan Kayqubad I, built in the 1220s on the southwest shore of Beyşehir with its own island retreat offshore. Only low walls and floor plans survive, but the star-shaped lustre tiles found here — double-headed eagles, peacocks, sirens, and drinking princes — are the finest Seljuk figural ceramics known, now in Konya's Karatay Medrese.
season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Oct — muddy access in winter
tip: See the Karatay Medrese tile collection in Konya either before or after, otherwise the site is just foundations by a reed bed.
todo: Trace the palace ground plan
Look across to Kız Kalesi island
See the tiles at Karatay Medrese
rev: Rewarding for anyone who has seen the tiles first; others describe an unstaffed, weedy enclosure at the end of a rough shore road with almost no interpretation.
onward: Konya (KYA) airport, then to Beyşehir and 35 km along the southwest shore towards Gölyaka; a car is required.

name: Meke Crater Lake
desc: A volcanic crater on the Karapınar steppe with a second, smaller cone rising out of the middle of it — a maar within a maar, once ringed by red salt water that photographed like a wound in the plain. Groundwater extraction has dried much of it; what remains is white salt crust, rust-coloured scoria and total silence.
season: Mar–May and Oct–Nov — summer heat and glare are punishing
tip: Do not expect the postcard water; go for the geology and the light, and stop at the viewpoint layby on the Karapınar–Ereğli road rather than driving down to the rim.
todo: Photograph the cone from the highway viewpoint
Walk the salt crust edge
Continue to the Karapınar obruks
rev: Still striking, but almost every recent report leads with disappointment that the lake has essentially dried up, and there are no facilities, shade or signage at the viewpoint.
onward: Konya (KYA) airport, then 100 km east on the D330 towards Ereğli; the crater is signposted just off the highway past Karapınar.

name: Karapınar Obruks
desc: Sinkholes punched straight down through the flat Konya plain, some old and green with water at the bottom, some collapsed last week in a wheat field. Kızören and Meyil obruks are the classic pair: near-circular shafts sixty to a hundred metres across with vertical walls and a disc of turquoise water far below. Unnerving to stand at the edge of.
season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Oct — the plain is 38 °C and shadeless in high summer
tip: Stay well back from the lips — the rims are undercut and actively collapsing, and there are no barriers at most of them.
todo: Look into Kızören Obruk
Find a fresh field collapse
Pair with Meke crater nearby
rev: Geologically fascinating and genuinely eerie, though visitors note dirt access tracks, no fencing or signage, and that the newer collapses are on private farmland.
onward: Konya (KYA) airport, then 95 km east to Karapınar on the D330; the obruks are scattered on farm roads and need a car.

name: İvriz Rock Relief
desc: A four-metre Neo-Hittite god of grain and wine holds out barley ears and a bunch of grapes to a small, praying king, carved into the rock beside a spring that still gushes into a poplar valley below the Taurus. The eighth-century BC hieroglyphs name Warpalawas of Tuwana. The water, the fig trees and the carving all belong to the same place.
season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Oct — the spring valley is a cool refuge in high summer
tip: Go in the morning; by afternoon the relief is in flat shade and the carved detail on the god's robe disappears entirely.
todo: Stand under the god and king relief
Follow the spring into the valley
Eat trout at a stream restaurant
rev: Consistently described as one of Anatolia's most beautiful reliefs in one of its prettiest settings, spoiled a little by picnic litter, loud weekend crowds and a scruffy car park.
onward: Konya (KYA) airport, then 150 km southeast to Ereğli and 17 km south towards Halkapınar; also reachable from Ereğli by taxi.

name: Ereğli
desc: A working plains town at the foot of the Taurus that most people use as a base for İvriz and Karadağ. Its own draws are quiet: a good small archaeological museum, the Akhüyük thermal mud pools, and a reputation across Türkiye for its cherries. The Taurus wall standing behind the flat wheat gives the place its horizon.
season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Oct — cherry season is late May into June
tip: Use it as a bed rather than a destination: İvriz, the obruks and Binbir Kilise are all within an hour, and Ereğli has the only decent hotels among them.
todo: Buy cherries in early summer
Visit the archaeological museum
Soak at the Akhüyük mud spring
rev: Practical and friendly rather than pretty; travellers mention limited evening options, a dusty industrial edge, and that the museum keeps short hours.
onward: Konya (KYA) airport, then 150 km east on the D330; Ereğli is also a stop on the Konya–Adana rail line and on all intercity buses.

name: Seydişehir
desc: An aluminium town with a surprisingly intact Ottoman core of flat-roofed stone-and-timber houses climbing towards the Taurus. It sits at the top of the spectacular road down to Antalya, and above it the Küpe mountain and the Suğla lake basin. The Seyyid Harun Veli mosque and its old quarter are worth the hour before you drive on.
season: May–Oct — the pass to Antalya can close in heavy winter snow
tip: It is the natural coffee stop before the Alacabel pass; fill the tank here, because the descent to Antalya has long stretches with nothing.
todo: Walk the old stone-house quarter
See the Seyyid Harun Veli mosque
Drive on over the Taurus pass
rev: Travellers who stop are pleasantly surprised by the old quarter; the town is otherwise dominated by the smelter and the historic houses are patchily maintained.
onward: Konya (KYA) airport, then 90 km southwest on the D695; frequent buses run from Konya, and it is on the Konya–Antalya road.

name: Derebucak Caves
desc: Karst country south of Beyşehir riddled with cave systems: Balatini with its lit chambers of stalactites, and Körükini and Suluin, where an underground river runs out of the rock into a wooded gorge. The forest here is cedar and juniper, the water is snowmelt cold, and the whole area sees a fraction of the visitors it merits.
season: May–Oct — the river caves are dangerous or shut in the wet months
tip: Take a jacket even in August; the show cave stays around 12 °C and the river cave mouth is colder still.
todo: Walk the lit gallery in Balatini cave
See the river emerge at Körükini
Picnic in the cedar forest
rev: Cool, uncrowded and genuinely scenic, but access is on winding forest roads, lighting and walkways are basic, and opening is seasonal and loosely enforced.
onward: Konya (KYA) airport, then 130 km southwest via Beyşehir on the Antalya road; a car is required for the forest approaches.

name: Yerköprü Waterfall
desc: The Göksu has cut a deep canyon south of Hadim, and at Yerköprü a tributary drops over travertine terraces into it in a curtain of white water hung with moss and fig roots. A natural rock bridge gives the place its name. The road in switchbacks down into the gorge, and the temperature drops as you descend.
season: Apr–Jun at full flow; Sep–Oct for warm water and low crowds
tip: The descent road is narrow with blind bends and no barrier in places — go slow, and use the lower car park rather than trying to turn round at the falls.
todo: Stand under the travertine curtain
Cross the natural rock bridge
Eat trout at the gorge restaurant
rev: People rate the setting highly, but flow drops sharply by late summer, the access road frightens some drivers, and weekend picnickers leave the riverbank littered.
onward: Konya (KYA) airport, then 130 km south via Bozkır to Hadim, then down into the Göksu gorge; a car is essential.

name: Obruk Han & Sinkhole
desc: A thirteenth-century Seljuk caravanserai standing on the empty Konya–Aksaray steppe, deliberately built beside a vast circular sinkhole whose water made the stop possible. The han is a plain fortified block of grey stone; the obruk beside it drops sheer to a dark green disc of water about a hundred metres down, with swallows working the shaft.
season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Oct — nothing but glare and heat in July and August
tip: It sits right on the old Aksaray road and is easy to miss at speed; look for the village of Obruk itself and the han is directly behind the houses.
todo: Walk the caravanserai courtyard
Look down into the sinkhole
Photograph the han against the steppe
rev: A satisfying stop on a long drive, though the han is often locked, the sinkhole rim is unfenced, and there is nothing at all in the village beyond a tea house.
onward: Konya (KYA) airport, then about 90 km northeast on the old Aksaray road via Obruk village; on the route between Konya and Cappadocia.

name: Taşkale Granaries
desc: A cliff above a village drilled with 250 rock-cut grain stores stacked in tiers, reached by notched footholds and wooden ladders, and still used by families to store wheat. From the road it looks like a honeycomb hanging over the houses. Some chambers are Byzantine rock churches reused; the whole face is one continuous vertical village.
season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Oct — the cliff face bakes in July and August
tip: Ask in the village tea house before climbing anything; some ladders are private property and the lower chambers are the only ones safe to enter without help.
todo: Photograph the honeycomb cliff
Climb to a lower granary chamber
Walk on to the Manazan caves
rev: Visitors describe it as one of the strangest things in Anatolia and almost unvisited, though there is no signage, no ticket office, and getting inside depends entirely on finding a willing villager.
onward: Konya (KYA) airport, then 110 km southeast to Karaman and 45 km east to Taşkale; minibuses run from Karaman but infrequently.

name: Manazan Caves
desc: A five-storey Byzantine cave settlement carved into a limestone cliff above the Ayrancı valley, with rooms, chapels and connecting shafts stacked one above the other. The mummified remains found here gave the top floor its name, Kilise Kat. Wind moves through the openings constantly, which is why the bodies dried rather than decayed.
season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Oct — the valley is fiercely hot in midsummer
tip: The internal stairs and shafts are unlit and worn smooth — take a torch, wear grip, and do not go up alone after rain.
todo: Climb through the connecting shafts
Find the chapel on the top floor
Look down the valley from the openings
rev: Adventurous visitors call it the best cave site outside Cappadocia; others report no railings, no lighting, no staff, and drops that make it unsuitable for young children.
onward: Konya (KYA) airport, then to Karaman and 40 km east on the Taşkale road; the cliff is signed off the road and needs a car.

name: Binbir Kilise
desc: On the black volcanic slopes of Karadağ, dozens of Byzantine churches and monasteries built from dark basalt stand roofless among the boulders and the sheep — the 'thousand and one churches' surveyed by Gertrude Bell in 1907. Some are barrel-vaulted shells you can walk into; the village of Madenşehri is built among them.
season: May–Jun and Sep–Oct — the mountain track is impassable in snow and mud
tip: Go to Madenşehri first for the concentration of standing churches, and take the higher Değle group only with a high-clearance vehicle or a local driver.
todo: Walk into a basalt basilica shell
Find carved crosses on lintels
Look out over the Konya plain
rev: Byzantinists rate it extraordinary and completely unvisited; the practical warnings are consistent — rough unsurfaced tracks, no facilities, sheepdogs, and no interpretation whatsoever.
onward: Konya (KYA) airport, then to Karaman and about 35 km north onto Karadağ via Dinek; a sturdy car and dry weather are needed.

name: Ermenek
desc: A town wedged under a vertical limestone wall in the deep Taurus, with a Karamanid mosque of 1302, stepped stone streets, and a castle on the crag above. Below it the Ermenek dam has flooded the Göksu canyon into a long turquoise fjord crossed by one of Türkiye's highest bridges. The drive in from any direction is the attraction.
season: May–Oct — mountain roads in and out are snow-affected in winter
tip: Approach from the Mut or Anamur side rather than Karaman if you can: the canyon road along the reservoir is one of the great drives in southern Anatolia.
todo: Drive the reservoir canyon road
See the 1302 Ulu Cami
Climb towards the castle crag
rev: Those who go rate the scenery highly, but the roads are long, winding and tiring, accommodation is very limited, and the town closes early.
onward: Konya (KYA) airport, then 110 km to Karaman and 150 km south through the Taurus; also reachable from the Mediterranean coast via Anamur or Mut.

name: Karaman Old Town
desc: Capital of the Karamanid emirate, the beylik that declared Turkish the language of the state in 1277, and still full of its patrons' buildings: the Hatuniye Medrese with its deep carved marble portal, the Yunus Emre mosque and tomb, the Aktekke, and a squat castle in a park. A serious concentration of fourteenth-century stone in an unshowy town.
season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Oct — the plain is hot and dusty in high summer
tip: Do the Hatuniye Medrese portal in morning light when the low sun rakes across the carving; by afternoon it is flat and the detail disappears.
todo: Study the Hatuniye Medrese portal
Visit the Yunus Emre tomb
Walk up to the castle mound
rev: A rewarding stop for anyone interested in pre-Ottoman architecture, though several monuments are locked outside prayer times and the modern town around them is plain.
onward: Konya (KYA) airport, then 110 km southeast on the D715; frequent buses and a rail link run from Konya in about ninety minutes.

name: Great Mosque and Hospital of Divriği
desc: In a small town at the far east of Sivas province stands the strangest stone carving in the Islamic world: four portals of 1228 covered in three-dimensional palmettes, sunbursts and vegetation so deeply undercut they cast shadows like foliage. Nothing else in Anatolia looks remotely like it. Inside, sixteen piers carry a vault over the joined mosque and hospital.
season: May–Oct — Divriği is high, remote and hard going in deep winter
tip: Come in raking morning or late afternoon sun; the flat midday light kills the relief that is the entire reason the building is on the UNESCO list.
wiki: Great Mosque and Hospital of Divriği
todo: Study the north 'Paradise' portal
Find the shadow-figure on the west door
See the hospital's carved central pool
rev: Architecture travellers call the journey worth it on its own, but long restoration campaigns have kept parts under scaffold for years and Divriği is a five-hour round trip from Sivas.
onward: Sivas (VAS) airport, then 170 km east; the scenic Sivas–Divriği train along the Kızılırmak is a better ride than the road.

name: Sivas Seljuk Madrasas
desc: Three thirteenth-century madrasas stand within a few hundred metres of each other on and around Konak Square: the Gök Medrese with its twin brick minarets and blue tile, the Çifte Minareli Medrese reduced to a single spectacular façade, and the Şifaiye, a hospital whose tiled tomb chamber holds Sultan Keykavus. No other Turkish city has this density of Seljuk work in walking distance.
season: May–Oct — Sivas sits at 1,285 m and winters are long and hard
tip: Walk them in one loop from the square in an hour, and check whether the Gök Medrese has reopened — it spent years behind restoration hoarding.
todo: See the Gök Medrese carved portal
Find Keykavus's tiled tomb
Photograph the Çifte Minareli façade
rev: Compact and impressive, with the standing complaint that the Çifte Minareli is now only a front wall and restoration closures are frequent and poorly announced.
entry: Free · small fee at the Şifaiye museum rooms
onward: Sivas (VAS) airport, 25 minutes from the centre; Sivas is also on the Ankara–Kars rail line and the new YHT route.

name: Balıklı Kaplıca (Doctor Fish Spa)
desc: A thermal pool on the bare Kangal steppe where two species of small fish strip the scaling from psoriasis sufferers who sit in the 35 °C water for hours a day. It has been a medical destination since the 1960s, with a spartan hotel attached and patients on three-week courses. Not a novelty pedicure — an actual treatment centre.
season: May–Sep — the site is remote and cut off in heavy winter
tip: Day visits are possible but the point is the multi-day course; book the on-site accommodation in advance because there is nothing else within 20 km.
todo: Soak with the doctor fish
Talk to long-stay patients
Walk out onto the open steppe
rev: Psoriasis patients report real results and a supportive atmosphere; casual visitors find the facilities dated, the location bleak, and the fish sensation unpleasant at first.
entry: Day entry roughly ₺400 (≈€8) · treatment packages priced separately
onward: Sivas (VAS) airport, then 100 km south towards Kangal and 13 km on a side road; a car or a pre-booked hotel transfer.

name: Kangal
desc: A high steppe district that gave its name to the massive fawn-coloured livestock guardian dog bred here for centuries to fight wolves. There is little to see in the town itself; the reason to come is the country around it — treeless rolling grassland, shepherds with their dogs and flocks, and long empty roads under enormous sky.
season: May–Sep — winters at 1,500 m are severe and roads drift shut
tip: Do not approach a working Kangal at a flock — they are guarding, not greeting; if you want to see the breed properly, visit the state breeding station rather than a roadside herd.
todo: See Kangals with a working flock
Drive the open steppe roads
Continue to the fish spa nearby
rev: Dog enthusiasts make the pilgrimage happily; others find the town itself drab, the breeding station's hours unpredictable, and the guardian dogs genuinely intimidating up close.
onward: Sivas (VAS) airport, then 100 km south on the D850 towards Malatya; Kangal is also a stop on the Sivas–Malatya railway.

name: Gökpınar Lake
desc: A spring-fed pool near Gürün so clear that the trout appear to hang in air above the pale gravel bed, ringed by willows in an otherwise dry, stony landscape. The water stays around 20 °C year-round and holds its blue-green colour through winter. Small, quiet and startling the first time you see it from the path.
season: May–Oct — the colour is strongest under midday sun
tip: Swimming is not allowed and the trout are protected; bring a polarising filter instead, or you will photograph nothing but sky reflection.
todo: Walk the lakeside path
Watch the trout over the gravel
Continue to Gürün's rock tombs
rev: Genuinely beautiful and rarely busy, but it is very small, the walk round takes fifteen minutes, and weekend picnic litter and roadside stalls have crept in.
entry: Free · small parking fee at weekends
onward: Sivas (VAS) airport, then 170 km southwest via Kangal to Gürün, then a few kilometres out of town; a car is needed.

name: Tödürge Lake
desc: A karst lake east of Sivas fed from below by springs, with reed islands that drift on the surface and shift position with the wind. Herons and grebes work the margins, the water is drinkably clear at the spring mouths, and the surrounding hills are bare and pale. Locals fish it from flat-bottomed boats.
season: May–Oct — it freezes over in a hard winter
tip: The floating islands are the local curiosity: ask a fisherman at Demiryurt village, and you may get taken out to one for very little.
todo: Look for the floating reed islands
Watch grebes at the spring mouths
Take a boat out with a fisherman
rev: A quiet, unexpectedly pretty stop on the road east, though there are no facilities beyond a tea shack and the shoreline is muddy and hard to walk in places.
onward: Sivas (VAS) airport, then 60 km east on the D100 towards Erzincan; the lake is visible from the highway near Demiryurt.

name: Şuğul Canyon
desc: A narrow green gash in the Kangal steppe: walnut and poplar trees, a cold stream, small waterfalls and rock-cut chambers in the canyon walls, all invisible until you are at the rim. After hours of treeless plateau the sudden shade and running water feel unreasonable. Local families come to picnic and to drink from the springs.
season: May–Sep — the stream runs low by late August, roads poor in winter
tip: The last stretch is an unpaved track through village fields; ask in Yellice for directions because the canyon is signed only intermittently.
todo: Walk the stream through the narrows
Find the rock-cut chambers
Picnic under the walnut trees
rev: Those who find it describe a small green paradise, tempered by a rough access track, no marked path beyond the picnic area, and weekend litter along the stream.
onward: Sivas (VAS) airport, then about 90 km south towards Kangal and onto village roads near Yellice; a car with clearance helps.

name: Yozgat Çamlığı National Park
desc: Türkiye's first national park, declared in 1958, and one of its smallest — a surviving stand of old black pine on a ridge above Yozgat that was once the town's private hunting wood. Some trees are over 500 years old. It is a park in the municipal sense as much as the wild one, but the pines are the real survivors of a forest that used to cover the plateau.
season: May–Oct for walking; Dec–Feb for snow under the pines
tip: Go on a weekday: at weekends the picnic areas fill with Yozgat families and the mangal smoke sits under the trees all afternoon.
todo: Walk among the 500-year-old pines
Take the ridge path for the plain view
See the Yozgat Çapanoğlu Mosque in town
rev: Pleasant, shady and historically interesting as the country's first park, but visitors note it is small, heavily used for picnics, and littered after busy weekends.
onward: Ankara Esenboğa (ESB) airport, then 220 km east on the D200; the park entrance is 5 km south of Yozgat town.

name: Sarıkaya Roman Bath
desc: A second-century Roman thermal bath excavated out from under a modern town, with the marble-lined pool still filling from its original hot spring and steps worn by Roman feet descending into the water. Known in antiquity as Basilica Therma, it stayed in use for centuries. The scale of the surviving pool and its rising steam catch people off guard.
season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Nov — the steam shows best on a cold clear morning
tip: Nobody has bathed here for a long time despite what the town's own signage implies; come to look at the masonry and go to a modern thermal hotel nearby to actually swim.
todo: See the spring still filling the pool
Walk the Roman pool steps
Look for the tentative-list information boards
rev: Impressive for a site so few people have heard of, though excavation and restoration are ongoing, walkways are makeshift, and opening hours can be improvised.
onward: Ankara Esenboğa (ESB) airport, then 260 km east via Yozgat towards Sorgun and Sarıkaya; buses reach Sarıkaya but a car is easier.

name: Çankırı Salt Cave
desc: A working rock-salt mine driven into a hill outside Çankırı, part of it opened as galleries of pink and grey salt carved into arches, a mosque and a salt-block dining room. The air is dry, still and around 16 °C, and asthma patients spend hours in the therapy chambers. Salt has been dug here since Hittite times.
season: Year-round — constant temperature makes it a good winter or heatwave stop
tip: Take a jacket and check the mine's visiting hours before driving out; it is an operating mine and public access closes without much warning.
todo: Walk the carved salt galleries
Sit in the halotherapy chamber
See the salt-block mosque
rev: A genuinely unusual hour and popular with families, but reviews mention limited English, a functional rather than scenic mine entrance, and queues on public holidays.
onward: Ankara Esenboğa (ESB) airport, then 130 km northeast on the D765; regular buses run Ankara–Çankırı in about two hours.

name: Ilgaz Mountain National Park
desc: The range that separates the Anatolian plateau from the Black Sea, rising to 2,587 m with fir and pine forest on the northern slopes and a small, cheap ski centre at Yıldıztepe. In summer the meadows above the treeline are full of wildflowers and the ridge walk gives you the plateau on one side and the sea haze on the other.
season: Dec–Mar for skiing; Jun–Sep for the meadows and ridge walks
tip: Ski here midweek — it is a fraction of Uludağ's price with short lifts and no queues, but weekends bring Ankara and Kastamonu day crowds all at once.
todo: Ski or sledge at Yıldıztepe
Walk the ridge above the fir line
Stop at the old Ilgaz pass road
rev: Well liked for value and forest scenery, with recurring complaints about short and dated lifts, thin snow in mild winters, and basic hotel food at the ski centre.
entry: Small national park vehicle fee · ski passes charged separately
onward: Ankara Esenboğa (ESB) airport, then 190 km north via Çankırı on the D765 towards Kastamonu; the ski centre is signed off the pass.

name: Kapulukaya Reservoir
desc: The Kızılırmak backs up behind a dam south of Kırıkkale into a long reservoir between bare ochre hills, with fishermen's shacks, a few tea gardens on the water and almost nothing else. It is not spectacular, but it is the one green line in an otherwise industrial province and the road along it makes a decent break on the Ankara–Kayseri run.
season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Oct — the hills are scorched brown by July
tip: Stop at one of the fish restaurants on the reservoir road rather than eating in Kırıkkale town, where the options are motorway-grade.
todo: Eat fish on the reservoir shore
Walk the Kızılırmak bank
Break the Ankara–Kayseri drive here
rev: Locals use it for weekend fishing and tea; travellers are honest that it is a pleasant pause rather than a destination, with scruffy shorelines and no real facilities.
onward: Ankara Esenboğa (ESB) airport, then 90 km east on the O-21 / D200 to Kırıkkale and south to the dam; a car is needed.
